title: PTGui Tutorial Part 1: Introduction — Panorama Basics, Workflow, and Parallax
summary: This opening PTGui tutorial frames what the software does, how panoramas are created, and the practical considerations when capturing images for stitching. It explains PTGui’s evolution from Panorama Tools, its built-in blender and stitcher, cross-platform availability, and the ability to output multiple projections (including Little Planet) and even gigapixel panoramas with GPU acceleration. The video then outlines the three-step panorama workflow (capture, stitch, present), how PTGui handles image layout, distortion, and blending, and discusses parallax as a core challenge. It ends with concrete shooting guidelines: use a panoramic tripod head, calibrate it, shoot manually with consistent exposure, prefer RAW for processing, and maintain adequate overlap while noting HDR considerations and lens correction responsibilities.

title: PTGui Tutorial Part 2 — Main Window, Panorama Editor, and Create Panorama
summary: This PTGui tutorial (Pro edition highlighted) introduces the main window user interface, contrasts PTGui with PTGui Pro, and demonstrates a quick panorama build from a set of images. It covers dragging images, using EXIF data for camera/lens inference, automatically aligning images, and opening the Panorama Editor. The video then walks through editing modes, levelling, and projection options, followed by trimming and viewing seams. It finishes with the Create Panorama tab, including output size optimization, export formats (JPEG vs Photoshop with layers), and common blending controls (Feather, Interpolator) along with how including or excluding images affects the final panorama. title: Levelling a panorama with vertical line control points in PTGui
summary: This PTGui tutorial (Part 8: Levelling) explains how to ensure a panorama is truly level when tripod leveling or Viewpoint Correction alone isn’t enough. It introduces a dedicated control-point type, the vertical line, placed on a real vertical feature in a single image to provide PTGui with a reliable vertical reference. The video demonstrates switching the control-point type from Normal to Vertical Line, placing at least two vertical-line points on a vertical edge (often top and bottom) and adding multiple points around the image to average out errors. It also covers using the Panorama Editor’s straightening tool, explains that straightening relies on yaw/pitch/roll, and shows how the optimizer uses vertical-line points to achieve a beautifully levelled equirectangular panorama. The session concludes with cautions about horizontal-line control points, which warp in the equirectangular projection, and notes a horizon exception where such a line might be appropriate.

title: Masking in PTGui Pro: painting, filling, and transferring masks across source images
summary: This PTGui tutorial explains masking as a Pro-level feature that defines which pixels from source images participate in the final panorama. It demonstrates selecting two overlapped images, using Edit Mask to isolate a specific area (a logo) so it is either fully included or excluded, and viewing seam placement with Show Seams. The video then covers painting the mask with red (exclude), green (include), and erase, plus using the fill tool and polygon drawing to quick-fill regions. It shows how masking affects seam position, how to zoom and adjust pencil size, and how to link/unlink images for synchronized masking. Finally, it demonstrates transferring masks between images, copying and pasting masks across multiple images, and saving/loading mask files for reuse. The examples center on how masking can remove a logo from a panorama and how the same mask can be applied consistently across a set of images.

title: PTGui Patch Tool Tutorial: Patching nadir/zenith and object removal in PTGui Pro
summary: This PTGui Patch Tool tutorial demonstrates how to fill gaps and remove unwanted objects in spherical panoramas using PTGui Pro. It covers two patching workflows: editing patch images externally with Photoshop or AI tools and using PTGui Pro's integrated Patch Editor. The example panorama is a fisheye shot from Iceland’s Geysir area, used to show handling nadir/zenith gaps, tone mapping, and seamless blending. The video explains patch image formats (TIFF, JPEG 2000, OpenEXR, JPEG), where patch images are saved, and how patches are incorporated into the project as dedicated sources with masks. It then walks through both workflows—external editor patching followed by automatic project reload, and a fully PTGui-centric Patch Editor approach—highlighting cut versus patch modes, hole creation, dragging patches, vertex edits, and seam visualization to achieve seamless blending.

title: PTGui Viewpoint Correction: Masking for Offset Images, Floor-Only Alignment, and a Cologne Cathedral Counterexample
summary: This PTGui Pro tutorial explains Viewpoint Correction, a feature used to integrate images captured from offset viewpoints (not at the no-parallax point) into a single panorama. The presenter emphasizes that the mapped area must be approximately flat, and demonstrates the workflow: enable Viewpoint Correction, mask everything not on the ground surface, then run Align Images and the Optimizer to verify results. A practical example shows masking the floor so only the flat surface is used, yielding a clean floor join; a counterexample (top of Cologne Cathedral) demonstrates the problems that arise when masking is not applied. The lesson underscores staying reasonably close to the no-parallax point to improve automatic control point generation and keep image deformation manageable.

title: PTGui Control Points Tutorial: Automatic Generation, Manual Refinement, and Masking for a 360 Panorama
location: Tunnel (explicit; photographed in a tunnel as stated in transcript)
summary: This PTGui tutorial explains the concept of control points, how automatic point generation works (in spirit similar to SIFT but not using SIFT in PTGui), and why manual refinement is sometimes necessary. The instructor demonstrates building a fresh project for a fully spherical 360° panorama from four tunnel images, showing how PTGui identifies corresponding points, the role of the cropping circle, and how to inspect, add, move, or delete control points. A control-point table is used to diagnose errors, after which the video covers optimization, removing outliers with the Delete Worst Control Points feature, and achieving a seam-free result with a well-calibrated tripod head. The session also introduces UI aids such as magnification, rectangular selection for group edits, masking to guide where points are generated, and generating points only between selected image pairs or within a masked region.
